en: Abhidhānottarottara 65.
[315.3] Now I shall further explain the sequence of the ritual for the physical form:
I am Locanā, the goddess Tārā, and Pāṇḍaravāsinī.
Mārīcī, Jambhara, Cūṇḍādevī, and Vasundharā—
each fully perfected from their own seed-syllable, endowed with twelve arms, three eyes, standing in the *ālīḍha* posture, and seated comfortably upon a being in the *sattvaparyaṅka* position.
Seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture,
naked, mounted upon a corpse, with loose hair and terrifying in appearance;
wearing a crown of garlands of skulls, she possesses the essence of compassion through her gaze directed from her lap.
The goddess Prajñāpāramitā is likewise the ground from which gnosis arises;
the self whose nature is the yoga of the form of Pratisarā is likewise firmly established in gnosis;
and the form of the wrathful Vajravidāraṇa likewise originates from the Hero.

Or else, having appointed the Hero Bhūtaḍāmara— who possesses a luster like split collyrium— as the presiding lord, one should meditate upon him through the state of one's own being and with the mind,
by means of non-concentrated yoga and through the process of analytical dissolution.
By means of the subtle *krodhavajra* in the center of the heart-lotus,
all *ḍākinīs* who perform the rites of their families dwell right here;
right here are all the perfectly awakened ones, the bodhisattvas, and the three worlds.

The worship of one's own self is the worship of the deities who are worshipped by all; if there were constant worship of the world, that is what was intended by the Jinas. By means of the vajra of internal yoga, the yoginīs are considered to belong to the Vajrins.
Therefore, [3] the wise one should perform worship with vajra-offerings;
through the application of the five offerings, one shall swiftly attain Buddhahood.
This reality which has been explained is considered the supreme external worship.
The cultivation of the form of the deity through practice, which is devoid of intrinsic nature, is considered the great worship that awakens all Buddhas.
The meaning of the tantras consists merely of such instruction; it is not the ultimate reality from the perspective of the highest truth.
That which arises from the ultimate truth is neither taught nor is there any teaching.
Since they are all established within the twenty-fourfold division beginning with the *pīṭhas*, those who possess the reality should not experience weariness through mere wandering.

If they were devoid of reality, there would be nothing for them due to their delusion; if they were endowed with the supreme state, there would be nothing for them due to their delusion. By serving the sacred seats (pīṭha), secondary seats (upapīṭha), and gathering places (chandoha), one becomes stainless.
Now, if a person is incapable or negligent regarding the recitation of the *pīṭhas*, then one should consider what we have said according to the disposition of sentient beings:
"There is no bliss higher than meditative absorption; therefore, one should be devoted to meditation."
The elements of those external yogins perish due to their delusion;
therefore, having set aside the external, one should abide in the play of yoga.
The Vajrayoginīs behold [reality] with the eyes of the twofold pure gnosis.
When they are pleased by the illustrious Vajrayoginī, whose mind is the essence of compassion, they present supreme accomplishments according to one's desire; therefore,
the Lord of Gnosis (Jñānabhaṭṭāraka) should be practiced with diligent effort.

The observance of conduct (*caryāvratam*) is proclaimed as being endowed with various forms of grace. Having set aside the observance of conduct here, one who delights in the observance of reality (*tattvavrata*) should,
by whatever means possible, establish the maintenance of his sustenance as a practitioner.
Devoted to the nourishment of meditative absorption, one should remain with the conduct of a madman—
whether naked or clothed, wherever and however one may be—
focusing upon one’s own tutelary deity and contemplating the single reality.
Within six months, he becomes subject [to mastery], and by virtue of attaining the state of silence,
that great yogi shines forth, attended by the yoginīs.
Having beheld the supreme light of gnosis, the yoginīs indeed worship him.

Just as swans enter a beautiful lotus pond, so too does one who possesses glory become Vajradhara manifest in this very life; of this there is no doubt. O Indrajālikavarṇākṣa, you are the accomplisher of the welfare of all sentient beings.
Having thus made this request of me, O pure-minded one, let it be done;
that which was spoken regarding her own internal organ will come to pass.
By means of the application of the wisdom-vajra, one should place it in the heart of the ḍākinī.
By means of the yoga of the heart-vajra hook, one illuminates the interior of the heart-vajra;
having placed the third vajra, one should contemplate the conceptualization of phenomena and the sphere of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
Bearing the form of radiant light, one should meditate through the yoga of the clear sky.
The arrangement of syllables of one’s own mantra, which is transparent and naturally stainless,
becomes the cultivation of the syllables of one’s own dharma through the yoga of one’s own mental disposition.
To whatever extent one might cultivate it in a different form through conceptual construction, [it remains so].
For that which is to be accomplished through the delusion of the mind, another arising is the faculty;
just as, through liberation, one may manifest form in a different way.
In the Abhidhānottara, this is the sixty-fifth chapter, on the worship of the physical body.
